newsitem.title: GERMANY: Activists use cement to block German nuclear train.
newsitem.headline: Activists use cement to block German nuclear train.

text.p: German anti-nuclear activists trying to block a controversial shipment of nuclear waste dug holes under a railway track on Monday and cemented their arms inside with quick-drying cement.
Police said the protest by two activists close to the train's destination of Dannenberg was delaying its arrival in the north German town.

Witnesses said the activists had dug holes under the track, thrust their arms inside and then poured in quick-dry cement. Police used picks and hammers but had not managed to pull the protesters loose three hours after discovering them.

The six contaainers of nuclear waste from southern Germany were expected to arrive in Dannenberg later on Monday before being transferred to trucks for the final stage of their journey to the Gorleben storage dump east of Hanover.
Police deployed in Germany's biggest post-war security operation said up to 2,000 activists had defied a ban on demonstrations along the route of the train and were camped around Dannenberg.

Militant protesters pelted riot police with stones. Other demonstrators played cat-and-mouse with police and border troops, disappearing when they arrived and then popping up to continue their obstruction.

Some activists set up burning barricades to block a road the truck convoy is expected to use. Others tunnelled under other parts of the likely route to weaken the road structure. Police said it was possible one road would have to be closed.
The train set off from the southern town of Walheim early on Monday and made its way northwards across Germany.
Some 30,000 police and border troops lined tracks along its route wearing riot helmets and carrying batons while police helicopters circled overhead.
The security operation will cost at least 66 million marks ($39 million) and surpass the 46 million marks spent on bringing a smaller shipment to Gorleben last year.

The containers were to be loaded on Tuesday on to flat-bed trailers in Dannenberg drawn by trucks to be taken by road to Gorleben, some 20 km (14 miles) away, where thousands more activists were camped and awaiting its arrival, probably on Wednesday.

Police said in general the protests were peaceful but local government officials condemned them. "Digging under roads has nothing to do with peaceful opposition," said Ulrike Wolff-Gebhardt, head of a town council in the Dannenberg area.
Greens Party leader Gunda Roestel told Saar radio her party valued the protests as "a symbol against atomic energy policy" and called for peaceful resistance.
"There is only one alternative for the (government's energy) concept -- to abolish atomic power in the face of popular protest," Roestel said.
Earlier, police removed anti-nuclear activists who staged a sit-down protest on rail tracks near the northern city of Goettingen, delaying the nuclear waste train for 20 minutes.
